The report also examined links between the TTP and other armed groups. Subsequent U.N. Security Council monitoring reports have provided further support for Pakistan’s security concerns. A July 2024 report noted that the TTP continued to operate from Afghanistan and conduct attacks inside Pakistan, citing member states’ assessments of Taliban tolerance and support for the group. The December 2025 report went further, describing the continued harboring of TTP leaders in Afghanistan and the facilitation of the group’s operations by the Taliban authorities. 
As concerns about cross-border militancy persisted, Islamabad pursued a parallel response at home. In June 2024, the government approved Azm-e-Istehkam, a national framework intended to strengthen intelligence-based operations and law enforcement. However, domestic counterterrorism measures have not resolved the cross-border dimension of the threat. 
Regional diplomacy has struggled to bridge the divide between Islamabad and Kabul. The eighth Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan, held on October 5, offered a recent example of this impasse. The meeting brought together Afghanistan and regional powers, including Pakistan, China, India, Iran and Russia, to discuss security and regional cooperation. It ended without a joint statement after the Pakistani and Afghan delegations struggled to agree on the language concerning terrorism. Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, emphasized the threat posed by militant groups operating from Afghan territory, while the Afghan Taliban delegation resisted the proposed wording. The disagreement illustrated a fundamental obstacle: the two sides have yet to agree on how to define and address the security problem itself.
The Moscow impasse followed earlier attempts to ease tensions through direct negotiations. After the October 2025 fighting, Qatar and Turkiye hosted talks that produced a ceasefire, followed by further rounds of negotiations in Istanbul, Doha, and Riyadh. These efforts did not resolve the central dispute. Pakistan seeks verifiable action against the TTP, while the Afghan Taliban authorities deny that the group operates from their territory in the manner Islamabad alleges. Without agreement on the underlying security concerns, diplomatic engagement has struggled to produce a durable settlement.
Economic ties have suffered as a result. In January 2026, Pakistani and Afghan traders agreed to establish a joint committee to discuss reopening border crossings. However, commercial negotiations could not overcome the wider security impasse. Since the October 2025 clashes, Pakistan has kept its border crossings with Afghanistan closed to trade – by far the longest closure in recent decades, disrupting a key transit route into Central Asia. The economic burden has fallen on traders and transporters on both sides, while Afghanistan has sought to diversify its trade through Iran, India, and other regional partners.
The costs of confrontation are therefore not confined to the security domain. Prolonged border closures disrupt livelihoods and commercial networks, while airstrikes and armed clashes expose civilians to further harm. The biggest challenge is to prevent the security dispute from becoming a self-reinforcing cycle in which militant violence prompts punitive measures, those measures deepen bilateral hostility, and deteriorating relations make cooperation against militancy even more difficult.
Breaking this cycle requires practical measures rather than competing declarations. First, Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban authorities could establish a verification mechanism, facilitated by a mutually acceptable third party such as Qatar, Turkiye, or China, to investigate specific allegations of militant activity and assess compliance with security commitments. Second, trade routes could be reopened gradually against measurable security benchmarks, linking economic recovery to demonstrable progress. Third, regional powers could support a sustained counterterrorism dialogue focused on information-sharing, specific incidents, and border management. Such targeted cooperation may offer a more realistic starting point than broader diplomatic forums where disagreements over the nature of the threat continue to prevent consensus.
On October 11, Pakistan’s military reported that security forces had killed 12 militants and Afghan Taliban personnel during an attempted crossing from Afghanistan into Pakistan’s Kurram district. A Pakistani soldier was also killed in the exchange of fire. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military’s media wing, said Afghan Taliban border posts had opened fire in support of the attempted crossing. 
The incident came 10 days after Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan, which Islamabad said targeted militant camps and hideouts. Pakistan reported that the strikes killed 22 militants. At the same time, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) confirmed that at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed and nine injured in Kunar and Helmand provinces. The U.N. mission called for de-escalation and greater protection of civilians, underscoring the humanitarian risks of continued cross-border hostilities.
Natasha Matloob is a journalist and analyst based in Islamabad, Pakistan, covering terrorism, militancy, security, and geopolitics across South Asia and the Middle East, with a focus on Pakistan, Afghanistan, India, and China. Her work has appeared in The Diplomat, World Politics Review, GIJN, the Stimson Center, and The Friday Times.
articles.summary: The costs of confrontation are not confined to the security domain; it’s impacting every facet of the bilateral relationship.

articles.title: Pakistan Imposes Emergency and Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
articles.full_text:
By invoking Articles 232 and 234, the federal government has essentially neutralized PTI’s institutional presence in the province.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Assembly building, Pakistan.
On October 11, Pakistan’s federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, which was being governed by former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).
The move, which was approved by President Asif Ali Zardari on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif following a federal cabinet meeting, marks a decisive takeover by the federal government of a province that has long been a PTI stronghold. The federal government justified the decision by pointing to a sharp surge in terror attacks across KP, alleging that the provincial administration was obstructing counterterrorism efforts, failing to maintain public order and allowing militant groups space to operate.
The federal government invoked Articles 232 and 234 of the constitution, which grant extraordinary powers to the federal government over provincial affairs.
However, the two articles address different circumstances and operate within distinct mechanisms. For instance, Article 232 empowers the federal government to declare a state of emergency when security is threatened by war or internal disturbance beyond the provincial government’s control. Under this provision, the provincial assembly continues to function, but federal laws take precedence in cases of conflict.
On the other hand, Article 234 allows the president to impose governor’s rule when a provincial government is judged unable to function in accordance with the constitution. Once implemented, the article suspends the provincial cabinet, transfers executive authority to the federal government or the governor, and permits parliament to exercise the assembly’s powers.
By deploying the two articles together, the federal government has essentially neutralized PTI’s institutional presence in the province. Article 234 has removed the PTI provincial cabinet and chief minister, which has effectively cut the party off from the province’s administrative system, official resources, and day-to-day levers of governance.
Moreover, Article 232 has shifted key legislative and public order authority to the center and provided federal authorities with stronger legal tools to enforce order, restrict street mobilization and limit any form of organized political activity.
By invoking Articles 232 and 234, the federal government has made a comprehensive effort to deny PTI any realistic prospect of regaining political or institutional influence in KP province in the near term.
This institutional confrontation is the culmination of months of friction between the federal government and PTI. The current setup in Islamabad is governed by a multi-party coalition, which is led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and supported prominently by the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) under President Asif Ali Zardari. It is pertinent to mention that after having assumed power following a highly contested election in 2024, the ruling coalition in Islamabad has remained engaged in an intense political feud with Imran Khan’s party.
The latest decision indicates that the relationship between the PTI-led provincial government and the federal government had become virtually unbridgeable.
From Islamabad’s perspective, the core dispute between the two sides centered on counterterrorism policy and the provincial government’s perceived defiance of federal priorities. It is important to note that security conditions in the province have deteriorated sharply in recent months with a marked rise in militant attacks.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Sunday went as far as saying that the PTI-led government had developed a nexus with terrorist groups and that a “power-sharing formula was gradually taking shape between terrorists and the PTI’s KP government, which was starting from southern districts and was ingressing further into the entire KP.”
The PTI leadership has questioned these assertions, arguing that security concerns are being leveraged to justify political measures aimed at diminishing the party’s footprint in the province. Furthermore, PTI leaders maintain that the central government refused to adopt a consultative approach to address the militancy challenge and also consistently denied party leaders access to consult with Imran Khan, who is languishing in prison.
The timing of this development is significant for many reasons. The emergency measures were imposed as the PTI prepared a long march from KP to Islamabad, the national capital, to demand Khan’s release from prison. Moreover, the provincial leadership, particularly Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, have refused to come on board the federal government’s counterterrorism policy. This stance hardened in recent months.
For decision makers in Islamabad, the provincial government had become both a political irritant and a security liability that was obstructing coordinated action against the militancy emanating from KP, which has become a threat to national security.
Following the declaration of emergency, one of the central government’s first administrative steps has been to establish a direct administrative framework for KP’s border and former tribal districts. The federal government has approved the immediate establishment of an Area Development Secretariat, which will be supervised by an Area Representative and Development Council and covers Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, and both Upper and South Waziristan. The ADS will be responsible for restoring law and order, protecting citizens, and ensuring governance and development.
Under this arrangement, civil administration, police and military coordination have been placed under a streamlined federal framework. It has created a more direct channel for Islamabad to manage high-risk districts. Moreover, this has also arguably reduced the scope for any future provincial government to impede security operations in these areas.
The move also carries clear external implications.
On Monday, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi stated that the days of lack of coordination between the center and the province on terrorism related issues are over, adding that “our policies will come from Islamabad … not Kabul, Jalalabad or Kandahar.” Arguably, Kundi’s statement was meant to emphasize that the state will not entertain dialogue or local deals with militant elements. By emphasizing that policy will originate from Islamabad rather than Afghanistan, he signaled that the federal government will no longer tolerate cross-border sanctuaries and will implement security policy unilaterally.
Kundi’s statement is important as it carries clear policy-level implications. If the new administrative framework is any indication, Pakistan is set to confront Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) threats and presence in its border regions more forcefully than before, and will likely pursue an uncompromising approach toward the Afghan Taliban on issues of militancy, border management, and cross-border sanctuaries.
One can argue that while the PTI government in Peshawar had become a political problem for the center, it had also evolved, in Islamabad’s assessment, into a security challenge. The party’s resistance to the measures now being imposed in the former tribal districts was viewed as untenable by both the federal government and the military leadership.
For now, the federal government has imposed its will in the province. Whether the new direct-rule arrangement can deliver improved security and reduced terrorist threats will determine whether it ultimately gains public acceptance. The immediate challenge for Islamabad is to ensure that the policy it is seeking to implement actually produces results on the ground.

articles.title: Indian IT Companies Are in Trump’s Crosshairs
articles.full_text:
Top companies like Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant will not be able to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers.
U.S. President Donald Trump is pressing home the advantage, as they say in sports. After showcasing the biggest advertisement for his stiff tariff policy against India — the Essar Group’s American subsidiary announcing an $18-billion investment in a U.S. steel project — Trump is going full throttle. This time, the target was Indian information technology (IT) companies.
On October 8, the U.S. suspended several companies from the Permanent Labor Certification Program, which allows firms to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers, saying the practice takes jobs away from Americans. The most affected companies are Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, and HCL.
U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the U.S. government would not accept or process any new or pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies.
U.S. journalist Fareed Zakaria said that Trump, a real estate developer, assesses who holds more leverage and pushes as hard and publicly as possible to dominate and extract the maximum price. Trump knows very well that the U.S. market is India’s Achilles’ heel.
The United States is a major destination for Indian goods, a crucial market for its IT companies, and an important source of employment opportunities for Indian professionals. Trump is using this leverage. The U.S. president, like the chief minister of any Indian state, is claiming that his tariff policies are bringing investment and manufacturing jobs to the U.S. He is welcoming foreign capital, not foreign labor. Vice President J.D. Vance said that the action was a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers at the expense of U.S. workers. His ire was directed at Microsoft, whose CEO, Satya Nadella, is of Indian origin.
According to Microsoft’s diversity data, Asian employees make up approximately 34.9 percent of Microsoft’s overall workforce. Some say a major chunk of this comprises Indians. This is why Vance lashed out at Microsoft, saying the company had abused the H-1B visa system to replace laid-off American citizens with foreign workers. He asserted that “no company in the United States, unfortunately, has abused this system more than Microsoft.”
The pressure is coming from several directions. On September 18, Trump signed a bill that gives him the power to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from countries that continue to buy Russian oil and natural gas. India is one of the world’s biggest importers of Russian oil.
One reason why India has avoided taking a confrontational position is that the United States is the only country with which India has a trade surplus, unlike China and Russia. India recorded a goods trade surplus of nearly $34 billion with the U.S., while the U.S. goods trade deficit with India reached $58.4 billion in 2025.
Trump has frequently criticized this imbalance, saying it has been “one-sided for years.” Trump argues that while India sells “massive amounts of goods” to the U.S., its largest client, high tariffs prevent reciprocal access for American companies. He has used the threat of tariffs to pressure India into opening its heavily protected domestic markets, such as its agricultural and automobile sectors, to American companies.
This is where Zakaria’s real estate analogy becomes particularly relevant. Trump has several points of leverage. But the question is: how far can India go in reducing the trade imbalance?
Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s statement in this regard is very significant. She said that trade talks with the U.S. had reached a plateau “beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult.”
This is the first time India has admitted to the pressure being exerted by the Trump administration.
Sitharaman said the U.S. wants to “reduce” its trade imbalance with India and wants to make up “for all that they’ve lost over these years.”
“When you’re talking of trade and trade imbalance being the sole criteria to reduce the imbalance, to what extent beyond negotiation can you go?” Sitharaman said.
This plateau has become a sort of war of attrition between India and the United States. How long it will continue, only time can tell. But the longer the stalemate persists, the greater the economic costs for both countries.

articles.title: Protests Escalate in Delhi Despite Modi Government’s Heavy-handed Crackdown
articles.full_text:
Indiscriminate arrests, detentions, police brutality, and blockades have not been able to demoralize protesters seeking the removal of the chief election commissioner.
A screenshot of a video posted by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) of a defaced hoarding of India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah during anti-government protests in New Delhi, India, Oct. 12, 2026.
On October 12, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, India’s main opposition leader, led a march to the Supreme Court of India, seeking the judiciary’s intervention in what he called the election commission’s loss of integrity.
The Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, had declined to meet the opposition delegation, arguing that it would violate the principle of separation of powers. Yet tens of thousands of people, including opposition lawmakers, activists, and ordinary citizens, marched towards the apex court premises.
Monday’s protest march drew unprecedented crowds, despite the Narendra Modi government’s brutal crackdown on protestors calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar, the first CEC to be appointed under a new law that allowed the government to pick an election commissioner of its choice, has been at the center of political controversies since the launch of a Special Intensive Revision of the electoral roll last year that has left millions outside the roll, leaving them at the risk of disenfranchisement. Opposition parties have alleged pro-government bias on a range of issues related to election conduct, including targeted voter roll manipulations.
Over the weekend, India stood witness to some unprecedented scenes. Police in the national capital of New Delhi raided hotels, hostels, the offices of political parties, and the residences of activists in search of suspected protesters. The goal was to foil the satirical youth network Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)’s October 10 protest in New Delhi. The CJP too is seeking Kumar’s resignation.
The CJP’s protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi in June-July resulted in Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. This time the Modi government was determined to prevent the CJP protests on Saturday.
To this end, it turned Delhi into a fortress. The assembly of five or more persons was prohibited across large parts of the city, and an estimated 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed. Police reportedly asked hotel owners to refrain from accepting fresh room bookings from people coming to the capital. To prevent protesters from gathering in New Delhi, the government took the unprecedented step of suspending or diverting dozens of Delhi-bound trains. Metro rail station gates closed across the city from 9 pm on Friday. Metal barricades blocked most roads leading to the designated protest venue, Jantar Mantar, in central Delhi. Checkposts multiplied at the city’s borders and Internet access was restricted in central Delhi. Early on Saturday morning, the police boarded a flight as soon as it landed in New Delhi to detain three CJP leaders. On Oct 10, Delhi was a city under siege. Daily life in the capital was suspended to prevent one political gathering.
And yet, thousands of protesters hit the streets in different parts of Delhi on Saturday. Thousands were detained, including lawyers, journalists, legislators and four former chief ministers of different states from the opposition parties. The police clashed with protesters at different locations. Young people on the streets were indiscriminately detained. Many alleged police brutality. Leftist student organizations kept cops busy on the streets on Sunday.
Even a U.N. human rights spokesperson expressed concerns over the situation, prompting the Modi government to accuse the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights of bias.
The Modi government may have been able to prevent youth and student protestors from gathering at one place on Saturday. But its problems are far from over, as the INDIA bloc and the CJP will be holding a wave of protests not only in the national capital but in other major cities as well. Besides, almost all opposition parties have thrown their weight behind the protests despite their internal rivalries – even if only for the time being. This has complicated matters for the Modi government.
“How long will you keep Delhi locked down? The minute you open the barricades & send police off, protestors will come in. Nobody, but nobody, can stop us,” said opposition parliamentarian Mahua Moitra on the night of October 10. The “government will never be able to ‘normalize’ life again.”
Meanwhile, a Supreme Court bench has directed the authorities to review their use of barricades, ensure normal metro and railway operations, and keep internet services running except where its suspension is legally justified.
By Monday, the government had adjusted its tactics. Instead of a citywide shutdown, it closed entry and exit at six central Metro stations from 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Delhi’s borders, railway stations, and bus terminuses remained tightly guarded. Traffic was diverted from selected roads. The government also denotified Jantar Mantar as a protest venue and designated three other places for protest purposes.
The CJP top leadership, who were released on Sunday, vowed to continue their protests. “If Modi thinks taking away Jantar Mantar [as a protest venue] will put an end to protests, he is mistaken,” said CJP founder-convenor Abhijeet Dipke, adding that Jantar Mantar was no longer just another location “but a spirit of resistance that nobody can ever take away.”
There does not seem to be an easy way out for the Modi government. It will not be easy for it to let CEC Kumar go. After all, Kumar is the Modi government’s appointee. Conceding ground here could encourage the opposition to aim higher next time.
On the other hand, if the opposition manages to maintain pressure on the government through intense and continued street protests, the credibility of the election commission could be further undermined in the eyes of the public.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has alleged that anti-national and foreign-funded forces have joined hands to destabilize the country. “We will deal firmly with all such forces active outside or inside the country,” said BJP president Nitin Nabin.
With the administration designating new locations away from central Delhi as protest venues and the opposition announcing continued protests, the coming few weeks look set for tense conflicts.

articles.title: Thailand Tightens Its Belt With 2027 Budget
articles.full_text:
The country’s budget planners have been wrestling with the same intractable challenge since the COVID-19 pandemic.
An aerial view of the Thai capital Bangkok at dusk.
Thailand’s budget for the 2027 fiscal year is out, and perhaps the most interesting feature is what it does not do: it barely increases spending at all. Approved expenditures came in at 3,788 billion baht, which is roughly $113 billion. This is a mere 0.2 percent increase compared to 2026, and marks the second year in which spending has been held just slightly above 2025 levels.
As a result of tighter spending, borrowing is expected to fall and the deficit is projected at 3.8 percent of GDP. This is tacit acknowledgement that the government is running out of policy space for prolonged deficits and more borrowing. A period of belt tightening, or at least an end to belt loosening, was not unexpected, and this budget seems to confirm that the time has arrived.
Budget planners in Thailand have been wrestling with the same intractable challenge for a few years now. The economy never fully recovered after the pandemic, remaining stuck in a low-growth equilibrium. With protectionist tendencies on the rise globally, and increasing competition from Vietnam, Thailand has struggled to export its way out of the economic malaise.
To make matters worse, Thailand has high household debt, which makes it difficult for consumers to drive an economic resurgence given constrained purchasing power. The digital wallet program was an ambitious attempt to jump-start the economy through an infusion of cash given directly to consumers, but it was not as effective as hoped for. It was also expensive and placed more pressure on Thailand’s capacity to run deficits and continue accumulating debt. As of March 31, 2026, total public debt was equal to 66.4 percent of GDP.
The 2027 budget suggests the government is now facing up to this reality by freezing spending. The ministries of transportation and agriculture are facing cuts, while police and military spending will hold steady. Capital expenditures are expected to fall. Health, education and social welfare will see small increases, but there are no major new and costly programs on the agenda. Revenue is expected to rise 3 percent. If all goes according to plan, and with spending held steady, this will provide an opportunity to start shoring up the fiscal situation which has been deteriorating since the pandemic.
In 2019, the Thai economy was doing well, which was reflected in its strong fiscal position. The economy was riding a years-long wave of current account surpluses thanks to booming exports. The budget that year forecast a fiscal deficit of 2.7 percent of GDP, but revenue came in higher than expected and actual borrowing ended up being just 2.1 percent.
The pandemic changed Thailand’s economic trajectory and its fiscal reality. In 2020 and 2021, Thailand ran large deficits as it borrowed money to fund stimulus programs and shore up healthcare and social protection systems. Every country in the region did the same. articles.title: The United States Has an Industrial Problem in the Indo-Pacific
articles.full_text:
A central part of the deterrence question
The littoral combat ship USS Freedom (LCS 1) transits the Pacific Ocean June 17, 2010, while enroute to participate in Rim of the Pacific (RIMPAC). RIMPAC is a biennial, multinational exercise in and around the Hawaiian Islands.
The United States has spent years warning about China’s growing military power. Much of that discussion focuses on ships, missiles, aircraft, artificial intelligence, and other weapons, but considerably less attention is paid to the industrial capacity behind them. China has built an enormous manufacturing base capable of producing ships, electronics, machinery, batteries, components, and other goods at a scale the United States cannot easily match. In a prolonged conflict, that difference could become as important as the capabilities of the weapons themselves. The United States would need to replace damaged equipment, replenish munitions, repair ships and aircraft, and keep production running under wartime conditions. Its allies in the Indo-Pacific would face similar demands.
Washington is increasingly aware of the problem and is trying to bring new companies, private investment, and manufacturing methods into the defense sector. The Navy’s recently announced Arsenal-2 project with Anduril Industries is one example. Announced October 6, Arsenal-2 is a planned $6.6 billion manufacturing facility at Tradepoint Atlantic in Maryland. Anduril plans to invest $3.7 billion of private capital, while the Navy could provide up to $2.9 billion. The facility is intended to manufacture components and large assemblies for Virginia-class submarines, initially including torpedo tubes and potentially expanding to larger sections of the boats. The project addresses a genuine weakness in the American defense-industrial base: the Navy needs more production capacity, particularly as it tries to expand the submarine fleet.
The difficulty is that Arsenal-2 will not be operational tomorrow. Initial operations are not expected until 2030, and the manufacturing methods that will underpin the facility still have to be developed and validated. Anduril will have to establish the workforce, suppliers, quality systems, and production processes needed to meet the demanding requirements of the submarine industry. That raises a broader question for Washington as it tries to rebuild the defense-industrial base: how quickly can the United States create industrial capacity that can actually be relied upon in times of crisis?
The question is particularly important in the Indo-Pacific. A conflict with China would place enormous demands on American production while US forces were operating thousands of miles from the continental United States. Ships would require repairs, missiles and drones would need to be replaced, and munitions stocks would have to be replenished. The United States would also be relying on its allies. Japan, Australia, South Korea, the Philippines, and other partners are increasing their defense capabilities, but American credibility in the region depends partly on whether Washington can continue supplying and supporting those forces during a prolonged crisis. A military that can deploy advanced systems but cannot replace them at the required rate has a very different deterrent value from one that can sustain production.
China’s advantage is not limited to the size of its military. Its civilian manufacturing base supports military production in ways that are difficult for the United States to replicate quickly. China is already a major producer of ships, electronics, machinery, industrial components, and many of the materials and products that underpin modern manufacturing. The United States, by contrast, is trying to rebuild capacity that has contracted over decades. This is why the defense-industrial debate should be viewed as part of the broader strategic competition with Beijing rather than simply as a question of Pentagon procurement.
That effort will require private capital and new companies capable of challenging established defense contractors. It will also require the government to create sufficient and predictable demand for companies to invest in factories, equipment, workers, and supply chains. The traditional defense industry cannot simply be expected to expand on its own after years of consolidation. At the same time, Washington cannot assume that every new company or manufacturing concept will succeed merely because it offers a different approach.
The Pentagon has considerable experience with the consequences of moving production ahead of development and testing. The F-35 is the most prominent example, while the Littoral Combat Ship provides another. The issue is not that these programs were necessarily wrong to pursue, but that the government has repeatedly faced substantial costs when production proceeds before key technologies and capabilities have been sufficiently demonstrated. A 2013 GAO review found that the F-35’s concurrent acquisition strategy had led to substantial rework costs as deficiencies were discovered in testing. A later GAO review found continuing delivery delays and recommended that the program better align incentives with production outcomes. The LCS program likewise faced significant operational and testing problems, including delays in developing mission modules.
Arsenal-2 presents a related question at the industrial level. The United States is investing in a new production facility while the manufacturing processes behind it are still being developed and validated. That does not mean Arsenal-2 should be delayed or that Anduril should not receive the opportunity to build it. The more useful question is how Washington structures the relationship. What production targets will the Navy require? How quickly must the facility reach them? Who will independently verify performance? What happens if production falls short? And can procurement shift toward other suppliers if a new approach does not deliver? Those are basic questions for any major defense investment, particularly when the United States is trying to rebuild capacity under pressure from a much larger industrial competitor.
There is a strong argument for taking risks on new defense companies. The existing defense-industrial base has its own shortcomings, and established contractors have not always been able to deliver new capabilities quickly or at the required scale. Private investors should be able to back companies they believe can change that, and Washington should encourage competition rather than protecting incumbents. But government support should not become a substitute for performance. Companies should have the opportunity to demonstrate that they can deliver, and successful performance should lead to greater opportunities. If a project fails to meet its targets, the government needs to retain the ability to limit further exposure and turn to alternatives.
There are precedents for Washington taking early risks on companies that had not yet demonstrated their full capabilities. NASA supported SpaceX before Falcon 9 had flown, while the Department of Energy provided Tesla with a $465 million loan in 2010 that the company later repaid. Some early bets work and some do not. The lesson is not that the government should avoid risk. It is that government needs mechanisms that allow successful companies to grow while preventing unsuccessful projects from consuming resources indefinitely.
That approach is particularly important when the objective is to compete with China’s industrial capacity. articles.title: Why China’s Training Center in Laos Will Not Change Vietnam’s Non-Aligned Foreign Policy
articles.full_text:
Hanoi’s best option to keep its western neighbors neutral is to resist further Chinese encroachment by political means.
A satellite image shows the construction of the China-backed air strip in Ban Keun, Vientiane province, Laos, Jan. 3, 2026.
China’s recent announcement of the opening of a new Joint Logistics and Training Center to train air force pilots in Ban Keun, Laos, has caused much concern about China’s intentions and capabilities. The new center, together with the China-Cambodia Joint Support and Training Center at Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, gives China’s military the ability to cover inland airspace over Indochina and out toward the Gulf of Thailand.
Vietnam has not commented on the new base at Ban Keun, but Prime Minister Le Minh Hung just concluded a visit to Laos and Cambodia. Laos was Hung’s first official visit since assuming the prime ministerial post in April. Hung and Thongloun Sisoulith, the president of Laos and general secretary of the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party, affirmed the “great friendship, special solidarity, comprehensive cooperation, and strategic cohesion” between the two nations. Both countries will celebrate the 50th anniversary of the signing of the 1977 Vietnam-Laos Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation next year.
China’s new base in Laos signals one of the major developments in Indochinese affairs since 1991. The 1991 Paris Peace Agreements ended the Third Indochina War and laid the basis for how China and Vietnam would handle Indochinese affairs to avoid a repetition of the polarization and arms race that contributed to Vietnam’s invasion of Cambodia in December 1978 and China’s retaliatory invasion of Vietnam in February 1979.
The Agreements demanded the withdrawal of foreign forces and their equipment from Cambodia, thereby ending the direct Vietnamese and Chinese interference in Cambodian affairs. This agreement came two years after China and Laos had normalized ties and three years after Vietnam began to withdraw its troops from Laos. China and Vietnam normalized ties in November 1991, the month after the Paris Peace Agreements. One of the key conditions of normalization is that neither country would seek hegemony in Indochina, which was the main reason China and Vietnam fought in 1979. After 1991, neither Vietnam nor China has had a permanent military base in Laos or Cambodia.
The post-1991 status quo is now enduring a stress test with the opening of China’s joint training centers in Ream and Ban Keun. From Vietnam’s perspective, what matters is not just the current capability but China’s future intentions. Although these centers are of limited military utility, China’s military presence could polarize Indochina if Laos and Cambodia come under pressure to host more Chinese military personnel or equipment, grant China exclusive access to these centers, or give China the right to use them during wartime. If Laos and Cambodia sided with China, it would completely expose Vietnam’s western flank to a hostile foreign power.
However, Vietnam will stick to its non-aligned foreign policy (no military alliances, no siding with one country against another, no foreign military bases, and no use of force or threats to use force in international relations) to maintain its goal of keeping Laos and Cambodia neutral.
If the Third Indochina War taught Vietnam any lessons, it is that allying with a great power to keep Laos and Cambodia in its orbit is not a viable policy option. In 1977, after the Khmer Rouge attacked Vietnam with tacit Chinese support, Vietnam began to side with the Soviet Union to counter Chinese influence in Cambodia.
However, Hanoi’s decision elevated what was a local issue between China and Vietnam into a great-power rivalry between China and the Soviet Union. China could not accommodate Vietnam’s interest in Cambodia and Laos and mediate the Khmer Rouge’s conflict with Vietnam when it perceived that Vietnam was ushering a great power into China’s backyard. Such an involvement made China determined to rid Indochina of any interference by linking Vietnam’s Indochinese ambitions with Soviet “socialist imperialism.”
Beijing accused Hanoi of colonizing its western neighbors and rallied world opinion against Vietnam. Vietnam’s alliance with the Soviet Union could not help it maintain its grip on Laos and Cambodia despite Moscow bankrolling the endeavor because Chinese military and economic punishments were too severe. After the Soviet retrenchment from Indochina in 1991, the neutralization of Laos and Cambodia was inevitable.
If Vietnam hosted a foreign military base on its soil to counter China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia, this would only make China double down on its presence. The Soviet presence at Cam Ranh Bay did not end China’s support for anti-Vietnam insurgents in Laos and Cambodia. There are simply no countries that can help Vietnam compete with China over Laos and Cambodia to the degree the Soviet Union could. The United States is not a continental power in mainland Asia. As such, Hanoi cannot abandon its stance of non-alignment.
It would also not be viable for Vietnam to threaten to attack China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia. This is not the first time China set up a joint training center in either Laos or Cambodia. In 1977, China helped the Khmer Rouge construct the 2,400-meter-long Krang Leav airfield in Kampong Chhnang, which at the time would allow China to station short-range bombers to carry out raids in southern Vietnam. China trained Khmer Rouge pilots and pledged to donate fifty-six aircraft to Cambodia. China also stationed engineering troops to construct roads in northern Laos beginning in 1962.
When Vietnam invaded Cambodia in December 1978, it quickly captured the unfinished Krang Leav airfield, thereby ending the Chinese threat from the southwestern front. Hanoi also captured Kampong Som (Sihanoukville), Cambodia’s only major seaport, through which it received Chinese war material. Although China did not send troops to Cambodia, Vietnam’s use of force against Cambodia gave Beijing the pretext to launch a retaliatory attack in February 1979. Laos subsequently ceased all cooperation with China, ending China’s military presence in Laos, but it did not restrain Beijing’s military punishment of Vietnam along the China-Vietnam land border and in the South China Sea.
It is not hard to imagine that Vietnam’s decision to use force against Ban Keun and Ream in the future would result in another Chinese attack. Vietnam can use long-range missiles to attack Chinese bases in Laos and Cambodia, which can spare the country of an invasion and limit escalation. However, there is no guarantee that China would not launch missiles against Vietnam’s bases or maritime outposts.
Because Vietnam can neither arms race nor side with a great power against China, Vietnam’s best option to keep Laos and Cambodia neutral is to resist further Chinese presence by political means. Vietnam’s friendship treaty with Laos should provide some degree of consultation between the two countries, as the treaty commits both countries to come to the defense of the other. Laos being transparent with Vietnam over the extent of Chinese presence and any future expansion plans would allay Hanoi’s fear to some degree. Vietnam’s affirmation of the 1991 Paris Peace Agreements and Cambodia’s constitutional clauses barring foreign bases from Cambodian soil remain vital. Like Laos’ case, Vietnam should press for more transparency over China’s presence at Ream. Vietnam should also highlight the continued trilateral cooperation framework among the three Indochinese countries to lock in the economic and political benefits of them cooperating with rather than siding against Vietnam.
Besides direct approaches toward its western neighbors, Vietnam can dilute the significance of Chinese centers by supporting more foreign presences there. The Ream Naval Base is a case in point. Although China funded the renovation and expansion of the base, Cambodia has invited foreign warships from Vietnam, Japan, the United States, Australia, India, and others to visit the base. If China’s center in Ban Keun is not directed against any third party, foreign countries should seek regular access to the center to refuel aircraft or exchange technical expertise with the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force. Vietnam’s diversified foreign policy means that it doesn’t matter which country visits the center, just that no countries are excluded from stopping at Ban Keun. This is how Vietnam’s foreign partners can help it achieve its objectives in western Indochina without alarming China.
Finally, Vietnam keeping its relationship with China amicable is the best method of keeping Laos and Cambodia neutral. Some observers have argued that the new bases in Laos and Cambodia signal a failure of Hanoi’s China policy. Despite Vietnam joining China’s “Community of Common Destiny” in 2023, these analysts claim, China is continuing the “encirclement” of Vietnam. However, this assessment downplays China’s largely non-confrontational stance toward Vietnam’s land reclamation campaign at sea. It is also worth noting that China calls the two facilities joint centers and not exclusive military bases, which signals a desire on Beijing’s part not to provoke Hanoi. Importantly, it is China’s air force and the navy that are at those bases and not the army, which would be more threatening to Vietnam. China has an interest in keeping its undisputed southern border with Vietnam stable while it focuses on Taiwan. In exchange, Vietnam must continue assuring China that it has no intention of siding with another great power against it. Such an assurance deprives China of any rationale to turn Laos and Cambodia against Vietnam.

Vietnam’s alliance with the Soviet Union could not help it maintain its grip on Laos and Cambodia despite Moscow bankrolling the endeavor because Chinese military and economic punishments were too severe. After the Soviet retrenchment from Indochina in 1991, the neutralization of Laos and Cambodia was inevitable.
If Vietnam hosted a foreign military base on its soil to counter China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia, this would only make China double down on its presence. The Soviet presence at Cam Ranh Bay did not end China’s support for anti-Vietnam insurgents in Laos and Cambodia. There are simply no countries that can help Vietnam compete with China over Laos and Cambodia to the degree the Soviet Union could. The United States is not a continental power in mainland Asia. As such, Hanoi cannot abandon its stance of non-alignment.
It would also not be viable for Vietnam to threaten to attack China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia. This is not the first time China set up a joint training center in either Laos or Cambodia. In 1977, China helped the Khmer Rouge construct the 2,400-meter-long Krang Leav airfield in Kampong Chhnang, which at the time would allow China to station short-range bombers to carry out raids in southern Vietnam. China trained Khmer Rouge pilots and pledged to donate fifty-six aircraft to Cambodia. China also stationed engineering troops to construct roads in northern Laos beginning in 1962.
articles.summary: Hanoi's best option to keep its western neighbors neutral is to resist further Chinese encroachment by political means.

articles.title: Malaysia to Raise Transboundary Haze Crisis With ASEAN Foreign Ministers Ahead of Summit
articles.full_text:
This year’s particularly severe haze season has once again exposed the void in national and regional efforts to combat the problem.
Thick haze obscures the sky above a residential area in Kalimantan, Indonesia, Aug. 20, 2026.
Malaysia’s government will raise the issue of transboundary haze at an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers’ meeting ahead of the bloc’s 49th Summit in Manila next month.
Over the past four months, massive wildfires have raged across Indonesia, particularly on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, causing a toxic haze that has seriously impacted Malaysia, Brunei, Singapore, and parts of the Philippines.
Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan told reporters in Sepang yesterday that the haze issue required special attention as it was not covered by existing ASEAN mechanisms for natural disasters, the state media agency Bernama reported.
“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he said. “So, this will be one of the issues that I will personally raise at the meeting with my counterparts.”
Air pollution from the fires, which have been prolonged and exacerbated by an unusually severe dry season, has forced the closure of schools across Malaysia in recent weeks. Last week, the government ordered schools to close in Melaka, Negri Sembilan, Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, and Putrajaya due to the worsening haze. The Malaysian capital rated among the world’s most polluted major cities globally. This came after hundreds of schools across the state of Sarawak on Borneo shut last month due to the hazardous air pollution in neighboring Kalimantan.
Malaysia has already been in touch with the Indonesian authorities about the fires. Last week, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that he had discussed the situation with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, who had “agreed to take the necessary steps.”
Mohamad Hasan said yesterday that Indonesia’s new foreign minister Arrmanatha Nasir had informed him that poor visibility in affected areas was hampering aerial firefighting operations. Many of the fires were also located deep inland, where water supplies were limited, and that some were in peatland areas, where fire-fighting is particularly challenging.
“Indonesia has between three to four aeroplanes and 34 helicopters, but they cannot take off because visibility is so poor that it is unsafe for any flights in the affected areas,” he said, as per Bernama.
Rizal Irawan, a senior official at Indonesia’s Environment Ministry, said last month that the country’s authorities were investigating 19 companies that it believes may be linked to the wildfires, and said it would investigate who might be responsible. Whether or not these investigations result in prosecutions and punishments remains to be seen.
“Transboundary haze” has become a seasonal crisis in large parts of Southeast Asia, much of it caused by agricultural burn-off on monoculture plantations, including palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar. These are compounded by vehicle and industrial emissions and naturally occurring dry season forest fires.
This year’s particularly prolonged haze season has once again exposed the void in national and regional efforts to combat the problem. Some nations have introduced their own legislation to tackle the haze problem, but effective enforcement requires support from the nation where the fires are located, something which has not always been forthcoming.
In 2002, ASEAN member states signed the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (AATHP), a recognition of the need “to co-ordinate national action for preventing and monitoring transboundary haze pollution.” In April, the 11-nation bloc inaugurated the ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control in Jakarta, which reflects member states’ “shared determination to achieve a haze-free region through stronger cooperation and faster response,” as Environment Minister Hanif Faisol Nurofiq put it at the time.
Much like the bloc’s human rights instruments, however, the AATHP and other ASEAN mechanisms are weighted heavily toward consensus and national sovereignty. As Rizky Ihsan of Griffith University put it in a recent article, “rather than restricting the states that signed up to it, the AATHP was designed to be acceptable to them.” Under the agreement, Rizky argued, “national governments have considerable control over how problems are reported, how emergencies are defined, and when outside help is requested.” He noted that similar issues also apply to the new Coordinating Center, which “will assist only when the national authority declares an emergency and asks for help.”
ASEAN is clearly aware that more effective regional mechanisms are necessary to combat the problem. Further discussions at next month’s ASEAN Summit to this end could be a welcome, if belated, move in this direction.
The challenge is that it not only requires cooperation between nations that often jealously guard their own sovereign prerogatives; it also, in many cases, requires confrontations with entrenched business interests that are unpalatable for national governments, and likely very challenging for regional mechanisms. Without serious coordination and a willingness to cede a degree of sovereignty in the service of the regional interest, Southeast Asia’s annual haze problem is only likely to continue.

articles.title: Philippine Lower House Passes Bill Restricting Social Media Access of Minors
articles.full_text:
If passed into law, the country will become the fourth in Southeast Asia to introduce youth social media restrictions of some kind.
The Philippine House of Representatives yesterday approved a measure barring children under the age of 13 from social media. It has become the latest nation in Southeast Asia to tighten online safety provisions for minors.
The Safe and Friendly Environment for Kids in Digital Spaces Act was passed nearly unanimously, with 287 lawmakers voting in favor and three against, Inquirer.net reported.
The measures align the Philippines with a growing global effort to restrict minors’ access to social media platforms, in the interests of protecting them from cyberbullying, online fraud, and exposure to pornography, among other perceived threats.
In the Philippines, the legislative push has come after a string of incidents of school violence that the government believes were driven by online content. Last month, a 16-year-old shot dead two fellow students and injured eight others at a school in the southern Philippines, before taking his own life.
This followed a similar incident in the same region in August, in which a student at a Catholic school live-streamed himself shooting and killing ​a classmate before taking his own life. Also in June, two students shot and killed three and injured seven of their peers at a school in Tacloban, allegedly in response to bullying.
Under the proposed bill, children aged 13 and below would be prohibited from creating social media accounts. Meanwhile, a variety of restrictions would be put in place for those under 18 years of age. They will be barred from making online purchases and engaging with “gambling-like mechanisms” and other features that may pose “reasonably foreseeable and material risks” to their well-being. They would also be shielded from harmful ads and algorithmic short-video feeds that encourage limitless scrolling, according to Inquirer.net.
Filipinos are heavy users of social media. The country has the sixth-largest pool of Facebook users in the world, with more than 102 million accounts registered, and an estimated 78.1 million TikTok accounts, the seventh-largest of any country. According to research, Filipinos spend an average of nearly 34 hours per week on social media.
Yesterday’s vote came after ⁠the Senate’s recent endorsement of a similar but slightly stricter bill, which would ban a minor under 18 years of age from registering, accessing, using, or maintaining an account on any age-restricted social media platform. According to Inquirer.net, the two dueling bills are now set for a “legislative showdown,” and it remains to be seen exactly what the final version of the legislation will look like.
These moves follow Australia’s introduction of the world’s first social media ban for under 16s. The policy, which took effect in December of last year, forces social media firms to block users under 16 from having accounts on their platforms, rather than penalizing young people or their parents. Despite the lingering questions about the effectiveness of such restrictions, a long list of countries, including India, China, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and several in Europe, have since followed suit and announced the introduction of curbs of some kind.
Within Southeast Asia, Indonesia in March became the first nation to ban under-16s from having accounts on what it termed “high-risk” digital platforms, including YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live, and Roblox. Malaysia started enforcing a similar ban on June 1, and ordered major social media platforms to conduct ​age verification against government-issued records. It has given them until January to ​implement the ⁠measure.
Vietnam also announced in July that it planned to introduce social media restrictions for minors. While Hanoi will not ban minors’ access to social media platforms, the new rules would bar under 16s from posting, commenting, sharing, or reacting to posts on social media.

articles.title: Wolf Warriors in Sheep’s Clothing: China’s New Subnational Diplomacy in Australia
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s diplomatic officials are adopting the language of the Albanese government to press their demands upon local governments and communities.
For the government of China, diplomacy is more than simply a means of cultivating international relationships and advancing national interests. It is also an instrument of regime maintenance. In this capacity it can take the form of coercive interventions in the domestic affairs of other states with the aim of suppressing conduct or critique considered hostile to the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Deploying diplomatic agents to secure compliance with CCP objectives is in fact a significant feature of China’s subnational relations with local governments and communities in Australia.
During Xi Jinping’s first decade as CCP general secretary and chairman of state, Beijing’s approach to Australia grew increasingly blunt and confrontational, a style known as “wolf warrior diplomacy.” More recently, Chinese diplomats have shifted to a quieter, more self-assured form of subnational diplomacy. In contrast to the bluster of the wolf warrior era, this approach is largely conducted behind closed doors and has become more evident since Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s July 2025 visit to China.
The election of the Albanese government in 2022 early signaled a thaw in what had been an icy bilateral relationship between Australia and China under the preceding Coalition governments of Malcolm Turnbull (2015-18) and Scott Morrison (2018-22).  On his second visit to China as prime minister, Albanese spent a week “stabilizing” relations through renewed business, trade, educational, cultural, and inter-governmental initiatives.  
Among the knock-on effects in Australia was a flurry of Chinese diplomatic initiatives at the local level. Consular staff in Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Perth now plainly assumed they were licensed by Albanese and his business entourage to press for local Australian compliance with their own demands on a range of issues. In meetings with local governments and peak community bodies, they carried a message: tolerating comments or events that displeased or offended the Chinese state or CCP would embarrass not just China or its ruling party, but the government of Australia. 
This was new. Rather than howling into the void, China’s diplomats were framing their demands in the Australian government’s own idiom. Wolf warrior diplomacy was giving way to “wolf warrior in sheep’s clothing diplomacy.” China’s officials were adopting the language of their hosts to press their demands upon local governments and communities. On evidence, to date the new approach is relatively effective but it carries risks for all parties.
A consular initiative in Melbourne undertaken shortly after the conclusion of Albanese’s trip to China shows the strategy in action.  In August 2025, China’s consul general in Melbourne requested a meeting with an independent non-profit organization that will remain unnamed. Its board welcomed the approach. This was not a low-key visit. The cluster of consular colleagues accompanying the consul general almost outnumbered the hosts around the table. 
During the formal presentation, the consul general reviewed Australia-China ties since 1972 and Melbourne’s consular opening in 1986. Past difficulties were behind us, he said. The Albanese government had corrected the errors of its Coalition predecessor. Canberra was restoring stability through trade, regional development, and people-to-people partnerships while recognizing China’s core interests – code for CCP rule and China’s claims over Taiwan, Tibet, Xinjiang, and the South China Sea, among other claims. 
The consul general then urged the board to read a recent article by iron-ore tycoon Andrew (Twiggy) Forrest, who predicted a bright future if everyone came on board the China boat. But, Forrest also warned: “Treat a friend like an enemy, and one day they may well become one.”  
A few locals around the table recalled hearing a similar warning five years earlier, when a Chinese diplomat presented a Canberra journalist with a list of 14 grievances, accompanied by the statement: “If you make China the enemy, China will be the enemy.” Most of those grievances presented in November 2020 concerned Canberra’s efforts to limit Chinese government engagement with subnational entities, on the one hand, and its failure to restrict independent Australian institutions critical of China and the CCP on the other.  China’s representatives in Australia appeared to be agitated not so much by the Coalition government’s external relations as by its domestic political arrangements governing the states and its failure to suppress commentary on China and its ruling party in Australia’s media, think tanks, and civil society.  
The public backlash to the “14 grievances” prompted China’s local representatives to park their threat for the time being. Events proved that they could afford to wait because the same warning would be reiterated by Forrest, one of Australia’s leading businessmen, in wake of Albanese’s visit.  
Having invoked Forrest, consular officials came up with a pointed request for the Melbourne board to cancel an event it was hosting with Australian journalist Cheng Lei. Cheng had been recently repatriated following three years in a Chinese jail for alleged spying activities. Giving her a platform to discuss her imprisonment, the Chinese diplomats implied, would undo all the good work of Albanese and his business team.
Despite the consul general’s request, Cheng’s talk went ahead. Nonetheless, China’s coercive interventions around her activities continued. Six months later, her play “1154 Days,” which recounted her solitary confinement and imprisonment in China, was dropped from Melbourne’s premier arts festival. “I feel like I’m back in China,” Cheng Lei told The Age.
Her concern was justified. The play had received a provisional place on the arts festival program, normally a routine step toward inclusion, but the board – not the festival’s creative staff – ruled against it. The RISING arts festival is funded through Creative Victoria and managed through the City of Melbourne’s Arts House, placing the festival program in a classic pincer movement between state and city governments known for their habit of surrender under consular pressure. 
Chinese government meddling in Victoria’s school textbooks, community organizations, Chinese-language media, and local government deliberations had been thought things of the past following the introduction of new federal laws around foreign interference in 2018 and legislation limiting state government overreach in foreign relations in 2020. Not so. 
Interviewed for this article, Cheng said that City of Melbourne officials received several consular calls and a personal visit urging them to avoid her play. Some did resist the pressure and attended. Arts House, for its part, was supportive of the work and kept the dates even though it wasn’t part of the RISING festival. The problem was not costs but the risks to the city and state governments’ relations with the local consulate
Cheng’s play was performed off-festival with support from a venue outside the City of Melbourne’s jurisdiction. There is a curious historical parallel here. In 1936 an anti-Nazi play was banned from city theaters in Sydney and Melbourne following representations from the German consulate, then under the direction of the Nazi Party. To their credit, the players found a way around the ban by performing on the back of a truck. 
For the fleet of Chinese consuls sailing in the wake of Albanese’s China visit, Melbourne was just one port of call. The Victorian consular team sought meetings with civic institutions and officials in Bendigo, Ballarat, Frankston, Geelong, and also Hobart in Tasmania, as well as with university executives and cultural institutions, including Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History. Consular officials based in Western Australia met up with local government officers in Perth, Joondalup, Cockburn, Gosnells, Geraldton, and Swan; Queensland-based ones visited Brisbane, Rockhampton, Mackay, Toowoomba, the Sunshine Coast, Gold Coast, and Southern Downs. The South Australian consulate paid visits to the local governments of Adelaide, Murray Bridge, and Clare Valley. In each state, consular officials also met with civic and community bodies.
In contrast to earlier consular tours, the nationwide consular outreach following Albanese’s visit drew little public attention. Not long beforehand, the Sydney consular team suffered public embarrassment when local newspapers reported on the consul general’s meeting with the mayor of Newcastle. At that meeting, the consul warned the mayor against the possibility of an AUKUS nuclear-submarine squadron possibly being based nearby, saying that this would harm China’s strategic interests. The mayor was reportedly taken aback to have been challenged on Taiwan, Tibet, and nuclear submarines – topics well outside the scope of Australian local government diplomacy – during a routine meet-and-greet with Chinese consular officials.
On Albanese’s return, consular teams adopted a quieter subnational style aligned with Canberra’s own “calm and measured” international diplomacy, which was explicitly contrasted with the former Coalition’s “bellicose megaphone diplomacy.”  Albanese’s approach, while helping to restore bilateral commercial, ministerial, and people-to-people ties at the national level, raised expectations on the part of China’s representatives in Australia that their demands for local discretion on sensitive matters would yield willing compliance. Canberra’s restraint was being repurposed to serve Beijing’s coercive subnational diplomacy.
It is doubtless clear to China’s diplomats in Australia that the Albanese government’s measured diplomacy has not altered Australia’s broader strategy in the region. This geopolitical strategy was inherited intact from the Coalition government and is aligned with regional partners’ understanding of the challenges and threats China presents.
That does not inhibit consular officials from cajoling local governments and community organizations to silence talk of those threats in the interests of stabilizing bilateral relations. In May 2026, Melbourne’s consul general told a local city newspaper that claims of “so-called” threats would “backfire” and rebound “just like a boomerang” on any making them. 
Backfire on whom? Most consular interventions have remained below Canberra’s threshold of awareness, but this is changing. In July 2026, Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History appeared to breach a federal funding agreement by hosting a consular speaker at its annual high-achievers program without notifying the government funding body. The rotating host for the 2026 Chinese Australian Achievers Awards was Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece of the City of Melbourne, which customarily invites China’s consular officials to speak at community events. By withdrawing funding, Canberra signaled its concern about consular officials piggybacking at federal expense on local events.
A more serious threshold was crossed later that month when the Museum first invited then disinvited Foreign Minister Penny Wong to launch journalist Emilia Tagaza’s book “Behind a Million Faces,” described by the Museum as “a seminal book on the history of Chinese Australians.” Wong accepted the invitation. Her office nominated September 1, 2026 for the launch, and it requested an advance copy of the book to be forwarded ahead of that date. 
In July, however, according to emails reviewed by the author, members of the Museum board reviewed their own advance copies and objected to its contents on several grounds. These included the author allegedly underplaying the U.S. factor in Australia’s deteriorating relations with China and overemphasizing communism, exaggerating China’s “assertiveness,” and incorrectly suggesting that Chinese migrants to Australia sought to escape CCP control. It directed the CEO to forward the author 17 pages of corrections, none of a factual nature, most entailing reframing  the agreed facts to minimize offense to the government of China. When Tagaza rejected the board’s amendments, the CEO was directed to cancel the launch and withdraw the invitation to the foreign minister.
That was not the end of it. The CEO reinstated the launch and Wong’s invitation after receiving advice that the board decision may have infringed the author’s free speech. Just weeks before the event, however, the board again reversed course and canceled the event and the invitation. September passed without the Museum book launch, and with the foreign minister wondering what on earth was happening in Melbourne.  
She had more than one reason to wonder. In 2024 a former Museum board member had become the first Australian to be jailed for planning foreign interference on behalf of the CCP – although not in his role on the board. But in fact nothing out of the ordinary was happening in Melbourne. Conspicuous displays of anticipatory obedience toward the local consulate are the default position among state and city governments, elite cultural institutions, and peak organizations in the city.  Given sufficient haranguing and inducement, institutions adapt their behavior to what they imagine local consuls want, in many cases without receiving specific requests. Self-censorship is commonplace.
The Museum too has a record of silencing voices and histories that could annoy China’s local officials. A small everyday instance of anticipatory obedience can be found in the Museum’s display on the recent history of immigration from China. A Museum volunteer told me that a draft text linked the 1989 Beijing/Tiananmen Massacre to Prime Minister Bob Hawke’s memorable offer of permanent residence after the massacre to tens of thousands of resident Chinese students. Were it not for the Chinese military’s slaughter of students and workers in Beijing, the 40,000 students would not have been invited to stay. The text on display elides this “offensive” context: “40,000 students arrived and studied whilst many stayed in Australia.”
More seriously, the Museum promotes certain histories while silencing others. The board raised no concerns before or after the launch in August 2026 of a book on the history of the Victorian branch of the Australia-China Friendship Society (ACFS), held at the Museum in association with events marking the 75th anniversary of that Society’s founding. The ACFS’s relationship with China is mediated by the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries under the direction of the CCP’s United Front Work Department. The consul general spoke at the historical commemoration along with Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece.  
What was novel in the case of Tagaza’s aborted book launch was not the selective censorship but censorship undertaken in full gaze of the Australian foreign minister. The board’s customary deference to China’s official perspectives on Australian history, immigration, and bilateral relations is not normally acted out in front of federal ministers. And this time the coercive influence over local government and community affairs wielded by China’s consulate in Melbourne embarrassed a senior member of Albanese’s Cabinet.
articles.summary: Beijing’s diplomatic officials are adopting the language of the Albanese government to press their demands upon local governments and communities.
